title: Combing cashmere from goats
subtitle: Cashmere is the soft undercoat that grows beneath a goat's outer guard hair. You comb it out in spring before the goat sheds it.
excerpt: Cashmere goats grow a fine undercoat through winter and shed it in early spring. A steel-toothed undercoat comb drawn through the coat in early March picks out the soft fibre before the goat loses it to fences and hedges. A full-grown cashmere goat yields 100-300 g of raw fibre per season, enough for spinning or felting.
sourceNotes: British Cashmere Producers Association technical guidance. Carla Emery, Encyclopedia of Country Living (1994), chapter on fibre animals. British Goat Society notes on fibre production breeds. Extension notes on cashmere goat management from Cornell Small Farms Program.

glossaryTerms.definition: The fine, soft downy undercoat grown by cashmere goats. Defined by fibre diameter below 19 microns. Grows through autumn and winter, sheds in spring. Distinct from the outer guard hair, which is coarser and longer.
The coarse outer coat of a goat, distinct from the cashmere undercoat. Guard hairs are long, straight, and not suitable for fine textile use. They must be separated from the cashmere after harvest.

content.text: has a natural shed point in early spring, typically late February to early March in the UK. The undercoat loosens from the skin in waves starting at the neck and working back. Comb the goat when you can feel the undercoat lifting, it comes free with a light pressure that the outer
resists. If you wait until April, the goat has already shed much of the fleece onto the field and your yield drops accordingly.

Blow gently against the grain of the coat on the neck and cheek. If the short, soft undercoat fibres lift separately from the long guard hairs, the cashmere is ready to harvest. If everything moves together, wait two weeks and recheck. On a cold spring the shed runs two to four weeks later than a mild one.
Work with the goat tied or held calm. Use a steel undercoat comb with tines set closely enough to catch the fine fibres but not so fine they pull the guard hairs.
Start at the neck and cheek, where the cashmere sheds first. Draw the comb through the coat in the direction of hair growth, applying enough pressure to go through to the undercoat.

Remove the gathered fibre from the comb tines with your fingers and place it in a clean bag. The first few passes bring up a mixture of cashmere and guard hair; subsequent passes become cleaner as the guard hair stays back.
Work across the neck, shoulders, and body in sections. The flanks give the most yield; the belly gives fine fibres but a smaller quantity.
Repeat the session 3-4 times over 2-3 weeks to capture the full shed rather than in one session.

Raw combed cashmere contains a mix of fine undercoat and coarser guard hair. Dehairing, separating the two, is time-consuming by hand. For home spinning, teasing the fibre out by hand and discarding obvious guard hairs is adequate. For commercial use, dehairing by machine is required; send to a British wool or fibre specialist for processing.

Store raw cashmere in a paper bag in a dry location. It keeps for a year or more without special treatment. Avoid storing with mothballs, the goat smell is natural and fades in washing; chemical smells from mothballs do not.
